analysis: Savi ugəró heavy, parãṛó white and lohĩló red have final written accent in the older comparative dictionary. They oppose the predominantly prefinal property-stem accent of Gilgit/Palula. These marks locate prominence but do not establish a surviving mora contrast. The newer source does not systematically transcribe stress, and the one-speaker Sawi pitch study suggests loss of a Palula-like lexical contrast, so historical versus source/dialect differences remain open.

Older Palula úguro/úṅguro heavy is initially accented across a three-nucleus stem, whereas current ungúru is prefinal. The prefix/cluster and quantity histories must be checked against the older primary source. This is retained as a genuine source/historical discrepancy, not made regular by deleting initial u.

Older Palula khā́čulo dirty/bad has an extra l-bearing extension relative to kháaču. Retaining the accent of the shorter stem before the extra suffix gives an independently plausible antepenultimate position. The precise derivational chronology is still unverified; no universal penultimate rule applies to all later extensions.

Kohistani khábooto left(direction) adds material beyond the ordinary khábo adjective. Preserved root stress before a directional extension gives antepenultimate prominence. Its grammatical function is explicitly directional, so it should not be treated as the same adjective citation cell.

Bagrot left kʰɑ̱ˈbo̱ and Hunza/Nagar short kʰu̱ˈṭo/kʰoˈṭo̱ have final survey stress despite the usual root-stressed forms. These are actual source-marked residuals. Elicitation intonation, speaker/dialect differences and transcription error are alternatives, but none is established without the recordings; do not overwrite them with the dictionary majority.

Nagar nɑˈu new and Hunza luˈʷo̱ red contain vowel/glide sequences with marked prominence. Exact syllabification and the role of the glide require source phonetic review before treating the marks as a final gender-suffix accent. They remain in the raw outcome inventory with a conservative sequence caveat.

Palula buṭhʹe and Haramosh buˈṭe all have a final e-bearing quantifier form, unlike Gilgit búṭo. Determine number/case and the quantifier paradigm before comparing them as one masculine adjective citation. The shared final e is an independent grammatical clue, not an accent correction.

Ushojo black is really written 'kinono in the checked raw source, with first stress over three vowel nuclei. Compared with Shina kíno, an extra -no or repeated stem ending could preserve the earlier stem accent and account for the apparent antepenultimate result. Its morphological function is unverified; retain the original form and the unresolved extra syllable.
